hidimbi.name: Hidimbi
hidimbi.description: A rakshasi of the forest beyond Varanavata who fell in love with Bhima and became his first wife. Sent by her brother Hidimba to lure the sleeping Pandavas to their death, she warned Bhima instead and later bore him Ghatotkacha. In the Kullu valley of Himachal Pradesh she is worshipped as the goddess Hadimba Devi.
hidimbi.story: After escaping the burning house of lac, the exhausted Pandavas and Kunti slept beneath a tree in a dark forest while Bhima kept watch. The man-eating rakshasa Hidimba, smelling human flesh, sent his sister Hidimbi to fetch them. But on seeing the mighty Bhima she fell in love, took on a lovely human form and begged him to flee with her. Bhima refused to abandon his sleeping family, and when the furious Hidimba arrived, Bhima wrestled and killed him. Hidimbi then turned to Kunti and Yudhishthira, pleading that she could not live without Bhima. Moved, they consented: she might roam with him by day and return him each night until a son was born. That son was Ghatotkacha, after whose birth Hidimbi departed, as agreed.
variations: The Critical Edition names her Hidimba, like her brother; the form Hidimbi is common in later retellings.
In Manali, Himachal Pradesh, she is venerated as Hadimba Devi, a goddess of the Kullu royal house, in a temple built in 1553; local lore says she renounced her rakshasa nature through penance there.

hidimba.name: Hidimba
hidimba.description: A man-eating rakshasa who ruled a forest near Varanavata and was the brother of Hidimbi. He was the first rakshasa slain by Bhima, in a ferocious wrestling match fought while the other Pandavas slept.
hidimba.story: Hidimba, a huge dark cannibal with tawny eyes and long fangs, sat in a sala tree in the forest beyond Varanavata. Catching the scent of humans, he sent his sister to bring them to him. When she lingered, having fallen for Bhima, he came roaring after her and threatened to kill her too. Bhima, not wishing to wake his sleeping mother and brothers, dragged the rakshasa away. The two grappled like maddened elephants, uprooting trees and raising clouds of dust until the others awoke. Arjuna offered to help, teasing Bhima for taking so long. Stung, Bhima whirled Hidimba overhead a hundred times, dashed him to the ground and broke him in the middle like a beast, and the forest was freed of its terror.
variations: In the Vana Parva the rakshasa Kirmira, slain by Bhima in the Kamyaka forest, names himself a friend of Hidimba and brother of Baka.

ghatotkacha.name: Ghatotkacha
ghatotkacha.description: The half-rakshasa son of Bhima and Hidimbi, named for his bald, pot-shaped head. He grew to manhood the day he was born, served the Pandavas whenever they called on him, and fell on the fourteenth night of the Kurukshetra war to the Shakti weapon that Karna had reserved for Arjuna.
ghatotkacha.story: On the fourteenth night of the war, when the fighting continued by torchlight, Ghatotkacha came into his own, for rakshasas grow stronger in the dark. Swelling to monstrous size and raining rocks, trees and weapons through a storm of illusions, he broke the Kaurava lines until Duryodhana's warriors begged Karna to save them. Karna held a single unfailing dart, the Shakti Indra had given him in exchange for his armour and earrings, which he had kept for Arjuna. With no choice left, he hurled it. The dart pierced Ghatotkacha's heart and returned to Indra. Even in death the rakshasa served his family, expanding as he fell and crushing a great host of Kaurava troops beneath him. The Pandavas wept, but Krishna rejoiced, for Arjuna was now safe.
variations: His son Anjanaparvan is killed by Ashwatthama in the Drona Parva; Barbarika as his son comes from the Skanda Purana and folk tradition.
His wife is unnamed in the Critical Edition; the Skanda Purana calls her Kamakantakata (Maurvi), daughter of Mura, while folk tradition calls her Ahilawati.
In the Telugu tale Sasirekha Parinayam (the film Mayabazar) he uses his illusions to win Balarama's daughter for Abhimanyu.
In Javanese wayang, Gatotkaca is a flying hero with muscles of wire and bones of iron, among the best-loved figures of the shadow theatre.

barbarika.name: Barbarika
barbarika.description: The son of Ghatotkacha, a peerless archer who in the Skanda Purana and in folk tradition gives up his head to Krishna before the Kurukshetra war. He does not appear in the Mahabharata itself. As Khatu Shyam he is one of the most widely worshipped deities of Rajasthan, Haryana and north India, called the support of the defeated.
barbarika.story: In the tradition centred on Khatu in Rajasthan, Barbarika, son of Ghatotkacha, was a matchless archer who had won three unfailing arrows: one to mark every target, one to destroy them all, and one to return to his quiver. Setting out for Kurukshetra, he vowed to fight for whichever side was losing. Krishna, disguised as a brahmin, tested him and saw that such a vow would make him swing endlessly between the armies until none but he survived. So Krishna asked him for a gift, and Barbarika, recognising him, offered his own head. Set on a hilltop, the head watched the whole war. Pleased, Krishna blessed him to be worshipped in the Kali Yuga under his own name, Shyam. In the Skanda Purana, Krishna instead strikes off his head to fulfil a curse from a former birth.
barbarika.vahana: A blue horse (Lila) in Khatu Shyam iconography
sources: Rajasthani and Haryanvi folk tradition (Khatu Shyam)
variations: He is absent from the Mahabharata; his story is a later Puranic and folk addition.

In the Skanda Purana he is a former yaksha reborn under a curse; he worships the goddesses at a sacred site, duels unknowingly with his grandfather Bhima, and Krishna beheads him with the Sudarshana; his head later testifies that only Krishna's discus truly fought the war.
In the Khatu Shyam tradition he freely gives his head as a gift (sheesh-daan); the three arrows are a gift of Shiva, and his head was found buried at Khatu and enshrined there.
His mother is Kamakantakata (Maurvi), daughter of Mura, in the Skanda Purana, and Ahilawati in folk versions.
A Nepali tradition connects the head-giving warrior with Yalambar, the Kirata king whose head is worshipped in Kathmandu as Akash Bhairav.

iravan.name: Iravan
iravan.description: The son of Arjuna and the naga princess Ulupi, raised in the serpent realm, who fought for the Pandavas and was slain by the rakshasa Alambusha on the eighth day of the war. In Tamil tradition, as Aravan or Koothandavar, he is the hero who sacrificed himself to Kali to ensure the Pandavas' victory, and he is the patron deity of the transgender (aravani) community.
iravan.story: Iravan was born in the realm of the nagas to Arjuna and the naga princess Ulupi, and grew up there, far from his father. When he travelled to Indra's heaven to greet Arjuna, his father embraced him and asked for his help in the coming war. On the eighth day at Kurukshetra, Iravan rode out with a host of swift horsemen and cut down several of Shakuni's brothers, the princes of Gandhara. Alarmed, Duryodhana sent the rakshasa Alambusha against him. The two fought through a haze of magic; Iravan's naga kinsmen rose to aid him in serpent form, but Alambusha took the shape of Garuda and devoured them, then struck off Iravan's head. Arjuna learned of his son's death only later, and grieved bitterly.
sources: Koothandavar temple tradition, Koovagam, Tamil Nadu
variations: In Tamil tradition (Villiputturar and folk dramas), he offers himself as a sacrifice (kalappali) to Kali before the war to ensure the Pandavas' victory; his last wish is to be married, and Krishna takes the form of Mohini to marry him and then mourns him as a widow.

At the Koovagam festival in Tamil Nadu, transgender devotees (aravanis) re-enact the marriage and widowhood; his severed head is worshipped as Koothandavar and, as with Barbarika, is said to have watched the whole war.
The Bhishma Parva calls his mother a daughter of the naga king Airavata, widowed when Garuda killed her husband, rather than the daughter of Kauravya as in the Adi Parva.

ulupi.name: Ulupi
ulupi.description: A naga princess, daughter of the serpent king Kauravya of Airavata's line, who drew Arjuna into the waters of the Ganga during his exile and bore him Iravan. Years later she engineered and then undid Arjuna's death at the hands of his son Babruvahana, reviving him with a naga gem and freeing him from the Vasus' curse.
ulupi.story: During his twelve-year exile, Arjuna came to Gangadvara, where the Ganga leaves the mountains. As he stepped into the river to bathe, Ulupi, daughter of the naga king Kauravya, seized him and drew him down to her father's palace beneath the waters. Arjuna calmly kindled the sacred fire and made his offerings, then asked who she was. Ulupi confessed that she had loved him at first sight and begged him to spend a night with her, arguing that saving a suffering being from death was itself dharma. Arjuna, bound by a vow of celibacy, yielded to her reasoning. At dawn she returned him to the riverbank and granted him a boon: he would be invincible in water, and every water creature would submit to him. Their son was Iravan.
ulupi.abode: The naga realm beneath the Ganga
variations: She explains in the Ashvamedhika Parva that the Vasus (with Ganga) had cursed Arjuna for killing Bhishma through Shikhandi; she had her father intercede, and the curse was discharged when Arjuna fell to his own son.
The Bhishma Parva describes her as a daughter of Airavata and a widow whose husband Garuda had killed.
When the Pandavas set out on their final journey, Ulupi entered the Ganga while Chitrangada returned to Manipura.
The Jaiminiya Ashvamedha expands her role in obtaining the gem that revives Arjuna.

chitrangada-manipur.name: Chitrangada (princess of Manipura)
chitrangada-manipur.description: The princess of Manipura, daughter of King Chitravahana, who married Arjuna during his exile on the condition that their son would inherit her father's kingdom. She was the mother of Babruvahana. Not to be confused with Chitrangada, the elder son of Shantanu and Satyavati.
chitrangada-manipur.story: Wandering through the east during his exile, Arjuna reached Manipura and saw the princess Chitrangada, daughter of King Chitravahana, and at once desired her. When he asked for her hand, the king explained a family peculiarity: Shiva had granted his ancestor Prabhanjana a boon that each generation would bear a single child, and his own was a daughter whom he had appointed as a son (putrika), so that her son would continue his line. Arjuna accepted the condition, married Chitrangada and stayed in Manipura for a time. When she bore a son, Babruvahana, Arjuna embraced them both, left the child as Chitravahana's heir, and resumed his journey. Years later she lamented over Arjuna's body when their son struck him down.
variations: The epic's Manipura lies near the eastern sea coast, close to Kalinga; its identification with modern Manipur is a later tradition, embraced by the Manipuri court after its Vaishnava conversion in the 18th century.

Rabindranath Tagore's play Chitra (1892) and dance-drama Chitrangada (1936) reimagine her as a warrior princess raised as a boy, who asks Madana (Kamadeva) for beauty to win Arjuna; this is a modern literary retelling.
After the war she lived at Hastinapura in the service of Kunti and Gandhari, returning to Manipura when the Pandavas set out on their final journey.

babruvahana.name: Babruvahana
babruvahana.description: The son of Arjuna and Chitrangada, raised as heir of his maternal grandfather and king of Manipura. During the Ashvamedha of Yudhishthira he fought his own father and struck him dead, and Arjuna was revived by Ulupi's naga gem, discharging the Vasus' curse for the killing of Bhishma.
babruvahana.story: When Yudhishthira's sacrificial horse wandered into Manipura, young King Babruvahana came out humbly with gifts to greet his father Arjuna, who was guarding it. Instead of blessing him, Arjuna rebuked him: a kshatriya should meet an armed intruder with battle, not bows of welcome. Then Ulupi rose from the earth and urged Babruvahana to fight. He donned golden armour, mounted his chariot and met his father in a fierce duel, until one of his arrows pierced Arjuna's chest and the great archer fell dead. Babruvahana collapsed in grief, and Chitrangada wept over her husband. Ulupi then brought a gem from the naga realm and laid it on Arjuna's breast; he rose as if from sleep, and Ulupi explained that this death had freed him from the Vasus' curse.
variations: In the Jaiminiya Ashvamedha, Babruvahana beheads Arjuna, and the revival involves a gem brought from the netherworld and Krishna's intervention.
Because Chitrangada was an appointed daughter (putrika), Babruvahana counted as the son of his grandfather Chitravahana's line rather than as a Kuru heir.
Babruvahana later attended the Ashvamedha at Hastinapura with his mother and Ulupi, where he was honoured by Kunti, Draupadi and Yudhishthira.

bakasura.name: Bakasura
bakasura.description: A powerful rakshasa who terrorised the town of Ekachakra, demanding a daily tribute of food, animals and a human victim. Bhima killed him while the Pandavas were living there in disguise as brahmins after escaping the house of lac.
bakasura.story: Disguised as brahmins, the Pandavas lodged with a brahmin family in Ekachakra. One day Kunti heard the family weeping: it was their turn to send the rakshasa Baka his tribute, a cartload of rice, two buffaloes and the person who brought them. Father, mother and daughter each offered to go in place of the others. Kunti, grateful for their shelter, declared that one of her five sons would go instead, and chose Bhima. Bhima drove the cart to Baka's forest, sat down and began eating the rice himself. The enraged rakshasa rained blows on his back, but Bhima calmly finished his meal before turning to fight. They uprooted trees and wrestled until Bhima broke Baka's back, and he left the body at the town gate, freeing Ekachakra.
variations: Kirmira, slain by Bhima in the Vana Parva, claims to be Baka's brother and seeks revenge.
Distinct from the crane-demon Bakasura killed by the child Krishna in the Bhagavata Purana.
Several places, including Ekchakra in West Bengal, claim to be the epic's Ekachakra.

mandavya.name: Mandavya
mandavya.description: An ascetic sage who was wrongly impaled as a thief and survived through his austerities. Learning that his suffering was punishment for tormenting an insect as a child, he cursed Dharma (Yama) to be born as a mortal, and Dharma was born as Vidura.
mandavya.story: Mandavya stood in silent meditation outside his hermitage, arms raised, under a vow of silence, when thieves fleeing the king's guards hid their loot there. The guards found the stolen goods, and when the sage would not answer, the king had him impaled on a stake with the thieves. Yet Mandavya did not die; sages came to him as birds, and the king, learning the truth, begged forgiveness. Unable to pull out the stake, the king cut it off, leaving the tip (ani) inside him, which gave him the name Ani-Mandavya. The sage then went to Dharma and demanded what sin had earned this. As a child, Dharma said, he had pierced a small insect with a blade of grass. Mandavya declared that no act before the age of fourteen should count as sin, and cursed Dharma to be born as a man, the son of a shudra woman.
variations: Some retellings set the age of accountability at twelve rather than fourteen.
In the Markandeya Purana, the impaled Mandavya curses the brahmin Kaushika to die at sunrise, and Kaushika's devoted wife halts the sunrise by the power of her fidelity.
The god he curses is called Dharma in the epic; later tradition identifies him with Yama.

kindama.name: Kindama
kindama.description: A sage who had taken the form of a deer to make love with his wife in the forest, and was shot by King Pandu while hunting. Dying, he cursed Pandu to die the moment he approached his wife in desire, which led Pandu to renounce his throne and made the divine births of the Pandavas necessary.
kindama.story: Pandu, the young king of Hastinapura, loved to hunt in the forests where he lived with his wives Kunti and Madri. One day he saw a stag and a doe coupling and brought them down with swift arrows. The stag was in truth the sage Kindama, who with his wife had taken deer form so as to enjoy love freely in the wild. Dying, Kindama reproached Pandu: even a cruel man does not strike creatures in the act of love, and a king who knew the scriptures should know better. He cursed Pandu that the moment he approached a woman in desire, he too would die. Grief-stricken, Pandu renounced his kingdom for the ascetic life. Years later, overcome by desire for Madri in the spring forest, he embraced her and died at once.
variations: The Critical Edition spells his name Kimdama; many popular retellings leave the sage unnamed.

nala-king.name: Nala (king of Nishadha)
nala-king.description: The virtuous king of Nishadha, son of Virasena, whose love for Damayanti, loss of everything at dice under the possession of Kali, and eventual restoration form the Nalopakhyana of the Vana Parva. The tale is told by the sage Brihadashva to console the exiled Yudhishthira, a fellow king ruined at dice.
nala-king.story: Twelve years after Nala won Damayanti, the demon Kali, furious that she had chosen a mortal over the gods, found his chance when Nala neglected to wash his feet before his evening prayers. Kali entered him, and Nala gambled away his kingdom to his brother Pushkara. Wandering the forest with Damayanti, half-mad, he tore their single garment and abandoned her as she slept. In a forest fire he rescued the serpent Karkotaka, who bit him, turning him into the misshapen Bahuka so no one would know him, while the venom tormented Kali within. As Bahuka, Nala served King Rituparna of Ayodhya as a charioteer, and traded his horse-lore for the king's secret of dice. With that knowledge Kali fled his body, and Nala reclaimed Damayanti and his kingdom.
variations: Shriharsha's Naishadhiya Charita, one of the great Sanskrit court epics, dwells on the courtship alone.
The gift of taste granted to him by Yama is the source of his proverbial fame as a cook; Nala-paka means a dish of rare excellence.
Distinct from Nala the vanara engineer who built Rama's bridge.

damayanti.name: Damayanti
damayanti.description: The princess of Vidarbha, daughter of King Bhima of Vidarbha (not the Pandava), who chose the mortal Nala over four gods at her svayamvara. Abandoned by him in the forest, she survived through wit and fidelity and contrived the second svayamvara that reunited them.
damayanti.story: A golden swan carried word of Nala to Damayanti, and she resolved to marry none but him. At her svayamvara, Indra, Agni, Varuna and Yama all took Nala's form, so that five identical Nalas sat before her. Damayanti prayed to the gods by the power of her truth: if she had never strayed from Nala in word or thought, let them reveal themselves. Moved, the gods showed their divine marks: they did not sweat or blink, their garlands stayed fresh, and their feet did not touch the ground, while the true Nala cast a shadow and his garland had begun to wilt. She garlanded him, and the gods blessed the marriage. Years later, abandoned and searching, she recognised her disguised husband by his gift for commanding horses and fire.
variations: During her wanderings she curses to death a hunter who tried to assault her, and serves the queen mother of Chedi as a maid before being recognised.
Her father, King Bhima of Vidarbha, is a different person from the Pandava Bhima.

savitri.name: Savitri
savitri.description: The princess of Madra, daughter of King Ashvapati, who married the exiled prince Satyavan knowing he was fated to die within a year, and won back his life from Yama through her persistence and wisdom. Her story, told by the sage Markandeya to Yudhishthira, made her the supreme model of the devoted wife and is honoured in the Vat Savitri vow.
savitri.story: On the day Satyavan was fated to die, Savitri, who had fasted for three nights, followed him into the forest. As he split wood he was seized with pain and laid his head in her lap. Then Yama appeared, dark and red-eyed, noose in hand, and drew out Satyavan's thumb-sized soul. As he walked south, Savitri followed. Yama urged her to turn back, but she spoke so wisely of dharma and friendship with the good that he offered her boons, anything but her husband's life. She asked for sight and his kingdom for her blind father-in-law, a hundred sons for her father, and a hundred sons of her own by Satyavan. When Yama granted the last, she pointed out that it required Satyavan alive. Delighted, Yama released him.
savitri.abode: Madra; later the kingdom of Shalva
variations: Married women observe the Vat Savitri vrata in the month of Jyeshtha, worshipping the banyan under which Satyavan lay.
She was born by the grace of the goddess Savitri, whom her father Ashvapati had worshipped for eighteen years, and was named after her.
Sri Aurobindo's epic poem Savitri reinterprets the tale as a spiritual allegory.

satyavan.name: Satyavan
satyavan.description: The son of the blind, exiled king Dyumatsena of Shalva, who lived as a forest ascetic and was chosen by Savitri as her husband despite being fated to die within a year. Restored to life by Yama through Savitri's devotion, he lived on with her for four hundred years.
satyavan.story: Satyavan grew up in a forest hermitage where his father, the blind King Dyumatsena, lived in exile after losing his kingdom. As a boy he loved to model horses in clay and paint them, and so was called Chitrashva. When the princess Savitri chose him, the sage Narada warned that, though truthful, generous and handsome, he would die in exactly one year. On that day Satyavan went into the forest with his axe to gather fruit and firewood, with Savitri at his side. Splitting wood, he felt a sudden agony in his head and fell asleep in her lap. When he awoke it was night, and he thought he had dreamed of a dark being carrying him away. Savitri told him she had brought him back from Yama.
satyavan.abode: A forest hermitage; later the kingdom of Shalva
variations: Some retellings reduce the number of boons Savitri obtains or change their order.

dhaumya.name: Dhaumya
dhaumya.description: The family priest (purohita) of the Pandavas, younger brother of the sage Devala, whom they chose at Utkochaka on the advice of a gandharva. He performed their household rites, married Draupadi to them, followed them into exile and taught Yudhishthira the worship of Surya that won the inexhaustible vessel.
dhaumya.story: When the Pandavas left Hastinapura for exile after the dice game, Dhaumya walked before them holding blades of kusha grass and chanting the grim Sama hymns sacred to Yama. Vidura explained the omen to Dhritarashtra: one day the Kurus would lie dead on the battlefield, and their priests would chant those same hymns over them. In the forest, when brahmins flocked after Yudhishthira and he grieved that he could not feed them, Dhaumya taught him the hundred and eight names of Surya. Yudhishthira worshipped the sun with them, and Surya gave him a copper vessel that would supply food each day until Draupadi had eaten. Before the year in disguise, Dhaumya counselled the brothers on how to live unrecognised at a king's court.
dhaumya.abode: Utkochaka tirtha; later with the Pandavas in the forest
variations: He is distinct from Ayoda Dhaumya, the teacher of Aruni, Upamanyu and Veda in the Adi Parva (Paushya Parva).
The gandharva who recommended him to the Pandavas is Angaraparna, formerly called Chitraratha.

bhima|hidimbi|spouse.label: Bhima married the rakshasi Hidimbi with Kunti's consent after killing her brother

hidimba|hidimbi|sibling.label: Hidimbi was the sister of the rakshasa Hidimba, who sent her to lure the Pandavas

bhima|hidimba|slayer.label: Bhima wrestled and killed Hidimba in the forest while his family slept

hidimbi|kunti|ally.label: Kunti accepted Hidimbi's plea and sanctioned her union with Bhima until a son was born

bhima|ghatotkacha|parent.label: Ghatotkacha was the son of Bhima by the rakshasi Hidimbi

hidimbi|ghatotkacha|parent.label: Hidimbi bore Ghatotkacha, who grew to manhood on the day of his birth

karna|ghatotkacha|slayer.label: Karna killed Ghatotkacha on the fourteenth night of the war with the Vasavi Shakti given by Indra, spending the weapon kept for Arjuna

krishna|ghatotkacha|ally.label: Krishna urged Ghatotkacha into the night battle and rejoiced at his death, since it spent the Shakti meant for Arjuna

ghatotkacha|draupadi|ally.label: Summoned by Bhima in the forest, Ghatotkacha carried the weary Draupadi and the Pandavas on the pilgrimage toward Gandhamadana

ghatotkacha|ashwatthama|enemy.label: Ashwatthama fought Ghatotkacha fiercely in the night battle and killed his son Anjanaparvan

ghatotkacha|abhimanyu|ally.label: In the Telugu tale Sasirekha Parinayam, Ghatotkacha uses his illusions to win Balarama's daughter for his cousin Abhimanyu
ghatotkacha|abhimanyu|ally.variation: Folk and regional tradition; not in the Mahabharata

ghatotkacha|barbarika|parent.label: Barbarika is the son of Ghatotkacha (and Maurvi or Ahilawati) in the Skanda Purana and folk tradition
ghatotkacha|barbarika|parent.variation: Not in the Mahabharata; the Skanda Purana names the mother Kamakantakata (Maurvi), folk tradition Ahilawati

krishna|barbarika|slayer.label: In the Skanda Purana, Krishna strikes off Barbarika's head with the Sudarshana before the war
krishna|barbarika|slayer.variation: In the Khatu Shyam tradition, Barbarika gives his head to Krishna as a freely offered gift (sheesh-daan)

barbarika|krishna|devotee.label: As Khatu Shyam, Barbarika is worshipped under Krishna's own name and is himself Krishna's devotee

krishna|barbarika|boon.label: Pleased by his sacrifice, Krishna blessed Barbarika to be worshipped in the Kali Yuga under the name Shyam

shiva|barbarika|boon.label: Folk tradition holds that Shiva granted Barbarika his three unfailing arrows
shiva|barbarika|boon.variation: Folk tradition; other versions credit the Goddess or Agni with his weapons

durga|barbarika|boon.label: The goddesses Barbarika worshipped granted him his invincible power
durga|barbarika|boon.variation: Skanda Purana (the Devis at a sacred site) and folk tradition

barbarika|bhima|enemy.label: In the Skanda Purana, Barbarika unknowingly duels his grandfather Bhima at a sacred pool until Shiva reveals their kinship
barbarika|bhima|enemy.variation: Skanda Purana; not in the Mahabharata

arjuna|iravan|parent.label: Iravan was the son of Arjuna by the naga princess Ulupi

ulupi|iravan|parent.label: Ulupi bore Iravan and raised him in the naga realm

iravan|shakuni|enemy.label: On the eighth day of the war Iravan slew several of Shakuni's brothers, the princes of Gandhara

iravan|duryodhana|enemy.label: Duryodhana sent the rakshasa Alambusha to kill Iravan after he routed the Gandhara princes

iravan|babruvahana|sibling.label: Iravan and Babruvahana were half-brothers, both sons of Arjuna born during his exile

iravan|kali|devotee.label: In Tamil tradition, Aravan offers himself as a sacrifice to Kali before the war to ensure the Pandavas' victory
iravan|kali|devotee.variation: Tamil tradition (Villiputturar, Koothandavar cult); not in the Sanskrit Mahabharata

mohini|iravan|spouse.label: In Tamil tradition, Krishna takes the form of Mohini to marry Aravan on the eve of his sacrifice
mohini|iravan|spouse.variation: Tamil tradition, re-enacted at the Koovagam festival

krishna|iravan|boon.label: In Tamil tradition, Krishna grants Aravan his last wishes: to marry, and for his severed head to watch the whole war

arjuna|ulupi|spouse.label: Ulupi drew Arjuna into the naga realm beneath the Ganga during his exile and became his wife

ulupi|arjuna|boon.label: Ulupi granted Arjuna invincibility in water and mastery over all water creatures; later she revived him with a naga gem
ulupi|arjuna|boon.variation: Ashvamedhika Parva: her revival of Arjuna discharged the Vasus' curse for the killing of Bhishma

ulupi|babruvahana|ally.label: Ulupi, Babruvahana's stepmother, urged him to fight Arjuna and then restored Arjuna with the naga gem

ulupi|chitrangada-manipur|ally.label: Arjuna's co-wives Ulupi and Chitrangada came together to Hastinapura and served Kunti after the war

ulupi|kunti|ally.label: After the war Ulupi lived at Hastinapura in the service of Kunti

arjuna|chitrangada-manipur|spouse.label: Arjuna married Chitrangada, princess of Manipura, on condition that their son inherit her father's throne

arjuna|babruvahana|parent.label: Babruvahana was the son of Arjuna by Chitrangada

chitrangada-manipur|babruvahana|parent.label: Chitrangada bore Babruvahana, heir to her father Chitravahana's kingdom of Manipura

chitrangada-manipur|kunti|ally.label: Chitrangada came to Hastinapura for the Ashvamedha and afterwards lived in the service of Kunti

babruvahana|arjuna|slayer.label: Babruvahana killed his father Arjuna in a duel over Yudhishthira's sacrificial horse; Arjuna was revived by Ulupi's naga gem
babruvahana|arjuna|slayer.variation: Ashvamedhika Parva: this death freed Arjuna from the Vasus' curse for killing Bhishma; in the Jaiminiya Ashvamedha, Babruvahana beheads him

babruvahana|yudhishthira|ally.label: Babruvahana attended Yudhishthira's Ashvamedha at Hastinapura and was honoured there

bhima|bakasura|slayer.label: Bhima ate the rakshasa's tribute of food and then killed Baka, freeing the town of Ekachakra

kunti|bakasura|enemy.label: Kunti, repaying the kindness of her brahmin hosts, sent Bhima in their place to confront Baka

mandavya|yama|curse.label: Wrongly impaled, Mandavya cursed Dharma (identified with Yama) to be born a mortal for punishing a child's act too harshly

mandavya|vidura|curse.label: Mandavya's curse on Dharma is the reason Dharma was born as Vidura, son of a shudra maidservant

kindama|pandu|curse.label: Dying, the deer-sage Kindama cursed Pandu to die the moment he approached his wife in desire

pandu|kindama|slayer.label: Pandu, out hunting, shot Kindama while the sage and his wife were mating in the form of deer

nala-king|damayanti|spouse.label: Damayanti chose the mortal Nala over four gods at her svayamvara

indra|nala-king|boon.label: At Damayanti's svayamvara Indra granted Nala the sight of his presence at sacrifices and a path to the highest worlds

agni|nala-king|boon.label: Agni granted Nala that fire would appear wherever he wished, and worlds as radiant as the god himself

varuna|nala-king|boon.label: Varuna granted Nala water wherever he wished and garlands that never lose their fragrance

yama|nala-king|boon.label: Yama granted Nala an unrivalled taste in food and steadfastness in dharma

kali-purusha|nala-king|enemy.label: Kali, enraged that Damayanti chose a mortal, possessed Nala and made him lose his kingdom at dice

karkotaka|nala-king|boon.label: Rescued from a forest fire, the serpent Karkotaka bit Nala to disguise him and torment Kali within, and gave him garments to restore his form

kali-purusha|damayanti|enemy.label: Kali vowed revenge because Damayanti had chosen a mortal over the gods

indra|damayanti|boon.label: Moved by Damayanti's truth-vow, Indra and the other gods revealed their divine marks so that she could choose the real Nala

agni|damayanti|boon.label: Moved by Damayanti's truth-vow, Agni revealed his divine marks at the svayamvara

varuna|damayanti|boon.label: Moved by Damayanti's truth-vow, Varuna revealed his divine marks at the svayamvara

yama|damayanti|boon.label: Moved by Damayanti's truth-vow, Yama revealed his divine marks at the svayamvara

savitri|satyavan|spouse.label: Savitri chose Satyavan as her husband though he was fated to die within a year

yama|savitri|boon.label: Won over by her wisdom and persistence, Yama granted Savitri boons culminating in Satyavan's life

yama|satyavan|boon.label: Yama restored Satyavan's life and granted him four hundred years with Savitri

narada|savitri|ally.label: Narada foretold Satyavan's death within a year, then approved Savitri's unshakable choice

dhaumya|yudhishthira|guru.label: Dhaumya, the Pandavas' family priest, taught Yudhishthira the 108 names of Surya that won the inexhaustible vessel

dhaumya|bhima|guru.label: Dhaumya served Bhima and his brothers as family priest (purohita) from the Adi Parva onward

dhaumya|arjuna|guru.label: Dhaumya became the Pandavas' purohita after Arjuna's encounter with the gandharva Angaraparna

dhaumya|nakula|guru.label: Dhaumya performed the household rites of Nakula and his brothers as their family priest

dhaumya|sahadeva|guru.label: Dhaumya performed the household rites of Sahadeva and his brothers as their family priest

dhaumya|draupadi|guru.label: Dhaumya kindled the sacred fire and performed Draupadi's marriage to the Pandavas, and accompanied her into exile
